paper.citation: Athey, S., Imbens, G. W. and Wager, S. (2018). Approximate residual balancing: Debiased inference of average treatment effects in high dimensions. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B (Statistical Methodology), 80(4), 597-623. DOI: 10.1111/rssb.12268.
paper.venue: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B (Statistical Methodology)
paper.source_locator: Section 5.2, unnumbered paragraph beginning 'To test the robustness of all the methods considered, we also ran a misspecified simulation'; printed p. 618, electronic-reprint PDF p. 22/27. Table 5 on printed p. 619, PDF p. 23/27 gives n={400,1000}, p={100,200,400,800,1600}; the paragraph itself has no numbered equation. Figure 2(b) on printed p. 616 illustrates the setting. ATE target and population truth are derived from the source outcome equation rather than reported numerically by the authors. Author R package balanceHD is cited in the article, but no code commit was run or claimed. Publisher-listed Supporting Information is described as proofs; its PDF was not accessible during this task.

mechanism.name: LaLonde-inspired misspecified treatment assignment with heterogeneous treatment effects

generation_equations.label: Covariates
generation_equations.expression: X_i ~ Normal_p(0,I_p), p=1600 in the selected Table 5 setting; all coordinates are independent standard normal.

generation_equations.label: Latent treatment intensity
generation_equations.expression: theta_i = log(1 + exp(-2 - 2 X_i1)) / 0.915; implement with stable softplus logaddexp. theta_i is latent and is not returned as an observed column.

generation_equations.label: Treatment assignment
generation_equations.expression: W_i | X_i ~ Bernoulli(1 - exp(-theta_i)); equivalently P(W_i=1|X_i)= -expm1(-theta_i) for stable numeric evaluation. This is the source's misspecified-setting mechanism, not an assumed logistic regression.

generation_equations.label: Observed outcome
generation_equations.expression: Y_i = sum_{j=1}^{10} X_ij + theta_i (2 W_i - 1)/2 + epsilon_i; epsilon_i ~ Normal(0,1). Cross-independence of epsilon is an implementation assumption pending review.

generation_equations.label: Potential outcomes / ATE
generation_equations.expression: Y_i(w)=sum_{j=1}^{10} X_ij + theta_i(2w-1)/2 + epsilon_i, w in {0,1}; Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)=theta_i; ATE=E[theta(X1)]≈0.389416787118157.

sampling.dependence: Individuals are iid under the implementation. Within an individual, X_j coordinates are independent standard Gaussian. The treatment W depends on X1 through theta(X1); the outcome depends on X1-X10 and the treatment-modified term theta(X1)(2W-1)/2. Outcome errors are drawn independently by implementation assumption; no clustering, repeated measures or interference.

assumptions: Consistency: the observed Y equals the potential outcome corresponding to observed W.
The potential-outcome interpretation keeps the same X and the same outcome disturbance epsilon under W=0 and W=1.

For this implementation, epsilon is sampled independently of X and W and across individuals; the source paragraph states its Normal(0,1) marginal but does not enumerate every cross-independence relation, so this implementation assumption awaits scientific confirmation.

Treatment is generated conditionally on X through the source probability 1-exp(-theta(X1)); this is strictly between 0 and 1 in exact arithmetic for finite X1, although numerical probabilities can round to boundary values at extreme inputs.
Individuals are iid in the implementation; covariate coordinates are mutually independent as specified by X~Normal_p(0,I_p). There is no interference.

properties.notes: This contribution implements the source-listed n=400, p=1600 setting, so p>n. The paper's Table 5 also includes n=400 and 1000 with p=100, 200, 400, 800 and 1600; variable p cannot be represented in one fixed observed-only schema by this checker, so the other grid points are documented but not separate scenarios here. Only X1 enters the nonlinear treatment mechanism through theta=softplus(-2-2X1)/0.915; X1 through X10 enter the additive baseline outcome. The treatment-effect heterogeneity is theta(X1), and the outcome term theta(X1)(2W-1)/2 includes W-by-theta(X1) effect modification. Nonlinearity is the softplus/exponential treatment mechanism, not an invented outcome interaction.

estimand.name: ATE
estimand.definition: Population average treatment effect E[Y(1)-Y(0)] in the synthetic superpopulation defined by Section 5.2's misspecified setting, comparing intervention W=1 with W=0 while holding the same pre-treatment X and outcome error fixed. The individual effect is theta(X1), so ATE=E[theta(X1)]. This is not ATT=E[theta(X1)|W=1].

truth.expression: Population average treatment effect E[Y(1)-Y(0)] in the synthetic superpopulation defined by Section 5.2's misspecified setting, comparing intervention W=1 with W=0 while holding the same pre-treatment X and outcome error fixed. The individual effect is theta(X1), so ATE=E[theta(X1)]. This is not ATT=E[theta(X1)|W=1].
truth.derivation: One-dimensional standard-normal expectation evaluated using 64- and 128-node Gauss-Hermite quadrature. A separately implemented composite Simpson integral over the standard-normal density on [-10,10] is used in verify.py. The reported error is a quadrature convergence diagnostic, not a formal uniform error bound.

adaptations: Select one source-listed Table 5 setting, n=400 and p=1600, because the collection checker requires a fixed observed-column schema across all configurations; the paper also reports n=1000 and p=100, 200, 400 and 800, which are documented but not separately implemented as scenarios in this contribution.

Make the population ATE target explicit by defining potential outcomes from the source's observed-outcome equation and holding X and epsilon fixed across interventions. The paper highlights that ATT exceeds overall ATE but does not provide an analytic numerical ATE value in this paragraph.
Compute E[theta(X1)] using Gauss-Hermite quadrature and independently verify with composite Simpson integration; this derives truth from the source DGP rather than copying a reported estimate.

The source specifies epsilon ~ Normal(0,1) but does not spell out every cross-independence relation in the misspecified-setting paragraph. The executable implementation draws epsilon independently of X and W and iid across individuals; this additional convention remains pending scientific confirmation.
Use a local NumPy RNG and vectorized sampling; this reproduces the specified distributions, not the original authors' random-number sequence.
